name: Jodhpur
tagline: The blue city beneath Rajasthan's mightiest hill fort.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Come in the cool winter, October to February, for clear desert light and the great fort festivals; avoid the fierce April-June heat entirely.

ourTake.lede: Jodhpur is really about one extraordinary fort and the blue city beneath it, so give the mornings to Mehrangarh and the late afternoons to wandering the indigo lanes of the old town. The rooftop-cafe view of the fort is worth chasing, but the fort itself, seen early, is the reason to come. Pair it with a night at a heritage palace and, if you have time, a village safari into the Bishnoi country.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the blue city, a mighty fort and a palace hotel that once housed a maharaja.
ourTake.skipIf: You want greenery or a beach; this is desert Rajasthan, dry and monumental.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan Palace
credentials: TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice, first Indian hotel named World's Best Hotel (2016); India's Best in subsequent years
MICHELIN Guide Hotel
Taj Hotels (IHCL) flagship palace
items.description: One of the world's largest private residences, half still the Maharaja's home, the first Indian hotel ever judged the best on earth.

items.name: RAAS Jodhpur
items.area: Old Blue City (near the Clock Tower, at the fort's foot)
credentials: World Architecture Festival (WAF) Barcelona 2011, World's Best Holiday Building
MICHELIN Guide Hotel
Aga Khan Award for Architecture, nominee (2013)
items.description: A 250-year-old haveli reborn in red sandstone and glass, Mehrangarh filling every window, the most design-led room in the city.

items.name: Ajit Bhawan
credentials: Recognised as India's first heritage hotel, Outlook Traveller
Former residence of Maharaj Ajit Singh of Jodhpur
items.description: India's very first heritage hotel, a 1920s royal residence, leafy and lived-in, where the palace idea began.

items.name: WelcomHeritage Bal Samand Lake Palace
credentials: ITC WelcomHeritage
Heritage palace of the Marwar royal house (Maharaja Jaswant Singh I)
items.description: A 17th-century red-stone summer palace on a 12th-century lake, 60 acres of orchards and birdsong, the city left behind.

items.name: Taj Hari Mahal
credentials: Taj Hotels (IHCL)
Palace-style heritage 5-star, Heritage Hotels of India
items.description: A Taj palace-style hotel on six acres of gardens, Rajput-Mughal grandeur, big-hotel polish, and the group's assured service.

items.name: Ranbanka Palace
credentials: Recognised heritage palace-hotel, Heritage Hotels of India
Erstwhile palace of the Jodhpur royal family
items.description: A 1920s Rajput palace between Mehrangarh and Umaid Bhawan, solid, characterful heritage without the icon's price.

items.name: Mehrangarh Fort
items.area: Fort hill, above the old city
items.description: The great Rathore stronghold Rao Jodha raised in 1459, rising 400 feet of sheer sandstone above the Blue City, its walls up to 36 metres high. Come at opening with a Mehrangarh Museum Trust historian and let the crowds arrive after you; the fort is a full unhurried morning, not a photo stop.

items.name: The Mehrangarh Museum galleries
items.description: One of India's finest private royal collections, kept by the Mehrangarh Museum Trust: palanquins and elephant howdahs, jewelled arms, Marwar miniatures, and the mirror-and-gold state rooms of Phool Mahal and Moti Mahal. The audio-guide is genuinely good, but a curator-led walk is what turns objects into your family's history.

items.name: The ramparts and cannon terraces
items.description: The high battlements where the old cannon still point out over a sea of blue rooftops, the desert horizon on one side and Jaswant Thada's white marble on the other. This is the view that made the Blue City famous; catch it in the soft light just after opening or before closing.

items.name: Flying Fox zip-line over Mehrangarh
items.area: Mehrangarh Fort ramparts and Rao Jodha Park
items.description: India's first heritage zip-line, six lines that launch off the battlements and fly over Ranisar and Padamsar lakes and deep into the desert park below the walls. A properly thrilling ninety minutes with a serious safety brief; a rare shot of adrenaline the older children and grandchildren will not forget.

items.name: Chamunda Mata Temple
items.description: The kuldevi shrine Rao Jodha carried from Mandore and installed at the fort in 1460, still the family deity of the Rathores and thronged at Dussehra. Its terrace is one of the best free viewpoints in Jodhpur, the Blue City falling away below and the fort walls rising gold behind you.

items.name: Jaswant Thada
items.area: Just east of Mehrangarh, above Devkund lake
items.description: The 1899 royal cenotaph of translucent Makrana marble, so finely cut the sheets glow amber in the sun; still the cremation ground of the Rathore rulers, set above a tiered garden and a small lake. Quieter than the fort and often golden at day's end, with resident musicians in the forecourt.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan Palace Museum
items.description: The public wing of one of the largest private residences on earth, the Maharaja's own Art-Deco palace, with clocks, arms, portraits and the family's story of the twentieth century. The lawns hold the royal vintage cars, Rolls-Royces and Cadillacs among them, a treat for anyone who loves great motoring.

items.name: Stay at Taj Umaid Bhawan Palace
credentials: World's Best
items.description: Still part-home to the Jodhpur royal family, the Taj-run wing is regularly named among the world's finest hotels, all Art-Deco grandeur, private butlers and 26 acres of gardens. The definitive multi-generational Jodhpur address; even non-residents can arrange high tea beneath the great dome.

items.name: Ghanta Ghar (the Clock Tower)
items.area: Heart of the old walled city
items.description: Maharaja Sardar Singh's landmark tower, its clock brought from England, standing at the centre of the old city as the fixed point everyone navigates by. Best seen in the last hour of daylight when the bazaar around it wakes up and the tower catches the low sun.

items.name: Sardar Market
items.area: Around the Clock Tower, old city
items.description: The great bazaar ringing the Clock Tower, alleys of spice, textiles, silver, lac bangles and antiques under the fort's gaze. Go early with a guide who can take you past the tourist stalls to the real merchants; the famed Mathania red-chilli mounds and mounds of saffron and dry fruit are a sensory event in themselves.

items.name: Old spice and textile shops of Nai Sarak
items.description: The lane where Jodhpur's families still buy their bandhej tie-dye, block-print and turban cloth, and where the old spice merchants blend and package to order. Ask a trusted shop to make up a personal masala box or a length of hand-dyed silk; a far better souvenir than anything airport-bought.

items.name: Toorji Ka Jhalra stepwell
items.description: A beautifully restored 18th-century royal stepwell, its carved sandstone tiers plunging into cool green water, built by a queen of Maharaja Abhay Singh. Free and open all day; the surrounding lanes have become the city's most charming little quarter of design shops and cafés.

items.name: The Stepwell Café and rooftop
items.description: The rooftop café looking straight down onto the stepwell and up at the fort, a relaxed spot for a long lunch or a coffee between the fort and the bazaar. Wood-fired pizza and cold drinks in a courtyard-and-terrace setting; the prettiest easy pause in the old city.

items.name: Blue City walk through Navchokiya
items.description: The oldest, bluest tangle of lanes, painted indigo since the Brahmin families first set their houses apart; every doorway and wall a frame. Walk it early with a local guide who is welcomed into the courtyards, and you see a living neighbourhood rather than a backdrop.

items.name: Brahmpuri lanes and rooftops
items.description: The Brahmin quarter climbing up toward the fort walls, its blue houses stacked steeply for the best rooftop views back at Mehrangarh. Time it for the golden hour, when the indigo deepens and the fort glows above the rooftops, then take chai on a family terrace.

items.name: Pachetia Hill viewpoint
items.description: A short climb from the blue lanes to a 360-degree panorama, the patchwork of indigo rooftops on one side and the fort crowning the ridge on the other. A quiet, local sunrise or sunset spot, well away from the tour buses.

items.name: Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park
items.area: Below the fort walls, around Devkund
items.description: Seventy-plus hectares of rocky desert ecology painstakingly restored beneath the fort, laced with walking trails past hidden lakes and 80-odd native plant species. Take a naturalist at opening for the birds and the cool of the volcanic-rock ravines; a serene counterpoint to the fort above.

items.name: Mandore Gardens
items.area: Mandore, 9 km north of the city
items.description: The old Marwar capital before Jodhpur, its temple-like red-sandstone royal cenotaphs rising out of green gardens, with the carved Hall of Heroes and shady walks. A leafy, atmospheric half-morning steeped in the dynasty's earliest history, with resident monkeys and far fewer visitors than the fort.

items.name: Kaylana Lake
items.area: 8 km west of the city, on the Jaisalmer road
items.description: A 19th-century royal-built lake ringed by low hills, best at sunset when the water turns to fire and, in winter, migratory birds gather. Boating and a quiet picnic; a soft, unhurried evening away from the old-city bustle.

items.name: Machia Biological Park
items.area: Near Kaylana Lake, west of the city
items.description: A well-run desert wildlife park beside Kaylana, jeep trails past Asiatic lions, leopards, blackbuck and gharial, with a good clifftop viewpoint over the lake. An easy, engaging couple of hours for families travelling with children.

items.name: Balsamand Lake and Palace
items.description: A 12th-century royal lake with a 17th-century red-sandstone summer palace on its bank, now a heritage hotel in sixty acres of fruit orchards and lawns. Come for a garden lunch or a lakeside dinner; a graceful, tranquil retreat that suits an unhurried afternoon.

items.name: RAAS Jodhpur rooftop and Baradari
items.area: Northeastern old city, below the fort
items.description: The city's original design hotel, built around an 18th-century haveli with every terrace framing Mehrangarh; the rooftop bar has the best fort-at-night view in town. Dine at Baradari in the old twelve-pillared pavilion, then watch the floodlit fort over a nightcap even if you are not staying.

items.name: Rajasthani thali at Gypsy
items.description: Jodhpur's beloved unlimited vegetarian thali, dal-baati-churma, gatte, ker sangri and a dozen Marwari dishes served till you wave the servers away. A generous, entirely veg feast, the honest, festive heart of Marwari home cooking.

items.name: Mirchi bada and mawa kachori at Janta Sweet Home
items.description: The institution for Jodhpur's own street sweets and snacks, the fiery mirchi bada, the rich mawa kachori, ghevar and rabri laddu, all pure-veg and made fresh through the day. Send someone ahead to bring a box back, or sit in for the full sugar-and-chilli education.

items.name: Makhaniya lassi and saffron at the Clock Tower
items.description: Jodhpur's famously thick, saffron-and-pistachio makhaniya lassi, served in clay cups at the old shops by the tower. A five-minute ritual that locals will tell you is non-negotiable; pair it with the market walk.

items.name: High tea at Umaid Bhawan
items.description: Afternoon tea beneath the palace's great Art-Deco dome or on the terraces over the gardens, open to non-residents by reservation. A slice of royal grandeur without an overnight stay; a memorable pause with children or elders who want the palace without the pace of sightseeing.

items.name: Jodhpur RIFF folk festival
items.description: The Rajasthan International Folk Festival, a UNESCO-backed roots-music gathering staged inside the fort under the brightest full moon of the year, dawn ragas on the ramparts and all-night concerts in the courtyards. Book fort accommodation and passes months ahead; the setting alone is worth the trip.

items.name: World Sacred Spirit Festival
items.description: A February festival of Sufi and sacred music split between Mehrangarh and the great Nagaur fort, an intimate, curated affair for those staying inside the forts. Access is limited and must be booked far ahead; deeply atmospheric for travellers who want the rarefied end of Rajasthan's culture.

items.name: Umaid Gardens and Sardar Government Museum
items.description: The city's leafy 82-acre public gardens below Umaid Bhawan, with a museum of Marwar sculpture, miniatures, arms and coins, and a small zoo. A gentle, shaded stroll and a cross-section of regional history; pleasant with grandparents and children in the cooler hours.

items.name: Bishnoi village safari
items.description: A jeep morning among the Bishnoi, the community who have protected the desert's blackbuck, chinkara and khejri trees for 500 years, and whose 363 martyrs died to save a grove. You meet potters, weavers and dhurrie-makers at work, and see herds of blackbuck grazing unafraid; the most moving cultural half-day near the city.

items.name: Kankani, the potters' village
items.description: A Bishnoi village where a master potter still turns a heavy stone wheel by hand to throw the region's clay vessels, often a stop on the safari. A quiet, genuine encounter with a craft that has not changed in centuries; children can try the wheel.

items.name: Salawas dhurrie weavers
items.description: The village famous for its handwoven cotton and camel-hair dhurries, made on pit looms by families who will weave a rug to your colours and size. Buy direct from the weaver and have it shipped; a craft purchase with a story attached.

items.name: Guda Bishnoi lake and blackbuck
items.description: A tranquil desert reservoir where blackbuck, chinkara and, in winter, demoiselle cranes and flamingos come to drink at dawn and dusk. A patient, beautiful wildlife hour, often paired with the Bishnoi safari, best with a good local naturalist.

items.name: Osian temples and desert
items.description: The 'Khajuraho of Rajasthan', a cluster of exquisitely carved 8th-to-12th-century Hindu and Jain temples, crowned by the hilltop Sachiya Mata shrine and the serene Mahavira temple. Pair the temples with a camel ride or sundowner on the dunes just beyond; a full, rewarding day-trip.

items.name: Marwari horses and riding at Rohet Garh
items.description: The 16th-century Rathore thikana of Rohet keeps one of India's finest stables of the ear-curled Marwari horse and runs everything from a dawn hack to multi-day riding safaris across Marwar. For riders, the definitive way to feel the region the way the Rathores did; Rohet Garh is a fine heritage stay in its own right.

items.name: Chandelao Garh and the women's craft cooperative
items.description: A restored village fort-hotel where the Sundar Rang women's cooperative produces hand-embroidered textiles and homeware, and guests learn block-printing and share village meals. A warm, grounded rural day that puts your spending straight into local hands.

items.name: Khejarla Fort day-trip or stay
items.description: A 400-year-old red-sandstone Rajput fort with carved jharokhas and lattice-work, now a characterful heritage hotel amid open countryside. Ideal as a leisurely lunch-and-village stop en route to Jaipur, or a quiet overnight with folk music under the stars.

items.name: Ahhichatragarh Fort, Nagaur
items.description: A vast, superbly restored 12th-century Rajput-Mughal fort of palaces, painted pavilions and ingenious water gardens, an Aga Khan award-winning conservation and the setting for the Sufi festival. A rewarding longer day-trip for those who want a great fort without the crowds, best paired with a stay at Ranvas within the walls.

items.name: Antique and curio hunting in the old city
items.area: Umaid Bhawan Palace road and old-city lanes
items.description: Jodhpur is one of India's great sources for antique and reproduction furniture, doors, silver and colonial curios, shipped worldwide by long-established dealers. Go with an eye and a trusted name; the city's dealers furnish collectors and designers around the world.

items.name: Lac-bangle and silver workshops
items.description: The tiny workshops where artisans still soften and shape coloured lac into bangles and set silver in the old Marwar way, tucked into the bazaar behind the Clock Tower. Watch a bangle made to order in minutes; a small, living craft you can buy at the source.

items.name: Cooking a Marwari meal with a local family
items.description: Several heritage homes and havelis host hands-on classes in the strictly vegetarian Marwari kitchen, ker sangri, gatte, bajra rotla and the sweets, followed by the meal you have made. An intimate way to understand a desert cuisine built without fresh vegetables; a favourite with families.

items.name: Hot-air balloon over the Blue City
items.area: Launch sites on the city's outskirts
items.description: Seasonal dawn balloon flights that drift over the sea of blue rooftops with the fort and desert spread below, a growing fixture in Jodhpur's cooler months. A once-in-a-trip aerial view; weather-dependent, so keep the morning flexible.

items.name: Ranisar and Padamsar lakes
items.description: Two linked medieval reservoirs tucked against the fort ramparts, built to water the citadel and now a peaceful pocket of green and birdlife glimpsed from the walls and the zip-line. A quiet detail most visitors miss; ask at the fort about access on the walking trails.

items.name: Jodhpur polo and the Rathore legacy
items.description: Jodhpur gave the world the jodhpur breech and a proud polo tradition, and the Rathore family still fields celebrated players; the winter season brings matches and the game is woven into estate life at Rohet and beyond. Arranged through the right hosts, a chukka or a match-day is a distinctively Marwari afternoon.

items.name: Risala
credentials: Inside Umaid Bhawan Palace, first Indian hotel named World's Best (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice 2016); MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Royal Marwari and Indian cooking from the Maharajas' own recipes, hung with martial portraits, the fort framed beyond the gardens, the grandest table in Jodhpur.

items.name: Baradari
credentials: Inside RAAS Jodhpur, World Architecture Festival 2011, World's Best Holiday Building; MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Contemporary and Rajasthani plates in an 1850s twelve-pillared pavilion, the floodlit fort towering above the courtyard, Jodhpur's most beautiful dinner.

items.name: Gypsy
credentials: Long-standing Jodhpur institution for the traditional Rajasthani thali
items.description: The definitive unlimited Marwari thali, dal-baati-churma, gatte, ker sangri, carried to the table till you surrender.

items.name: Janta Sweet Home
items.area: Old Blue City (near the Clock Tower / Sardar Market)
credentials: Long-standing Jodhpur sweets & snacks institution
items.description: Jodhpur's kachori legend, pyaaz and mawa kachoris, ghewar and mirchi vada, a bazaar rite of passage.

items.name: Shri Mishrilal Hotel
items.area: Old Blue City (Sardar Market, by the Clock Tower)
credentials: Established 1927, the original makhaniya lassi house (Sardar Market)
items.description: The makhaniya lassi that made Jodhpur famous, saffron, cardamom and a cap of clotted cream, poured here since the 1920s.

items.name: Trophy Bar
credentials: Inside Umaid Bhawan Palace, first Indian hotel named World's Best (TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice 2016); MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: A cabinet of colonial curiosities and hunting trophies, rare whiskies, cigars and quiet royal elegance, the grandest nightcap in the city.

items.name: Stepwell Café at RAAS
credentials: Inside RAAS Jodhpur, World Architecture Festival 2011, World's Best Holiday Building; MICHELIN Guide Hotel
items.description: Three tiers above the floodlit Toorji stepwell, Mehrangarh looming behind, an evening cocktail with the best view in the old city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Jodhpur, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive at Umaid Bhawan Palace, the Taj-run Art Deco residence still home to the royal family, and settle before the heat.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A curator-led afternoon at Mehrangarh Fort, ending on the ramparts as the blue city glows below.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Cocktails at the Umaid Bhawan bar, then dinner at Risala over the palace gardens.

days.label: Day 2
days.title: The old city and its makers

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A guided walk through the Sardar Market lanes and the blue houses of the Brahmpuri quarter with a local historian.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Visit the marble Jaswant Thada cenotaph, then an afternoon at the RAAS Jodhpur pool beneath the fort.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Baradari at RAAS on the terrace, with Mehrangarh floodlit above you.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive into the Bishnoi villages for block-printing, pottery and a tea with a farming family, arranged privately.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Rohet Garh heritage house, then a slow return across the scrub.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner under the stars at Umaid Bhawan, or a quiet in-suite meal before departure.

items.name: Old Blue City (below the fort)
items.description: The indigo lanes and rooftop cafes; best for atmosphere and the classic fort views.

items.name: Umaid Bhawan / palace side
items.description: Grand and secluded on the ridge; suits those wanting palace grandeur and calm.

items.name: Ratanada / newer town
items.description: Quieter and residential with mid-range comforts; for a practical, less touristy base.

events.name: Rajasthan International Folk Festival (RIFF)
events.note: A superb roots-music festival staged inside Mehrangarh Fort on the October full moon.

events.name: Marwar Festival
events.note: A two-day celebration of Marwari folk music and dance honouring the region's heroes.

events.name: World Sacred Spirit Festival
events.note: An intimate festival of devotional and Sufi music held within the fort.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The blue city glows with lamps beneath the floodlit fort, a striking sight from the rooftops.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Mehrangarh Fort is the anchor, go early and take a guide. Stay in the old blue city for atmosphere or at Umaid Bhawan for grandeur; summer heat is severe, so plan sightseeing for morning and evening.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Jodhpur Airport (JDH), a civil enclave about 15 minutes from the old city, and take a chauffeured car; Raas, the Taj Umaid Bhawan and the Raas Devigarh set-ups will send a car to meet you.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver for the fort and the desert edge, and slow walking through the blue lanes of the old town beneath Mehrangarh.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: 4G is solid in the city and hotel wifi is good; an Airtel or Jio eSIM before you land is the cleanest option.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Indian rupee (INR); cards work at hotels and established shops, cash for the bazaars, tipping around 10 percent.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to March is the good stretch: warm days, cool nights, the blue city sharp under clear skies. Avoid April to June, when desert heat pushes past 42C, and the July-September rains.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi (approx 1h20m), Mumbai (approx 1h45m) and Bengaluru (under 2.5h) into Jodhpur Airport (JDH); IndiGo flies all three, Air India and Akasa on Delhi. A compact civil-enclave airport, so keep connections generous and let the hotel handle the pickup rather than expecting a lounge.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine Hep A/typhoid cover. Safe, relaxed city. Sealed or filtered water; the desert air is dry, so drink more than you think.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Simple for vegetarian and Jain guests; Marwari food is vegetarian by tradition and no-onion-no-garlic cooking is standard. The dining rooms at Umaid Bhawan Palace and RAAS do polished vegetarian Rajasthani; dal-baati-churma is the local staple.
